stops.name: The finca, the marriage to Pietro di Bernardone
stops.campa: Pietro di Bernardone asks for the hand of Giovanna called Pica, of the illustrious house of Bourlémont, and the family consents to the merchant. The contract is drawn, sealed, and laid up in the archives of Provence, the parchment Father Frassen will one day affirm he held in his hands. She is dowered richly; on her dowry the fortune of the Assisi shop will be founded. The halls of the finca fill a last time with her family's singing; Pierre sings the fifth suffering. Then the bride turns east with the wedding train, a Bourlémont bound for Umbria.

stops.name: Montgenèvre, over the roof of the cloth road
stops.campa: The cloth road crosses the Alps at Montgenèvre, the merchants' pass, gentle enough for laden mules. Pica rides over the roof of the road between France and Italy carrying her true dowry in her saddlebags: the Persian poems of Ganja, a Provençal songbook, the romance of the knight and the lady Fée, and the five sufferings with their five remedies. On the height the carters point out the watershed: behind her the Rhône and the Meuse, before her the Po and the roads of Lombardy and Tuscany. The magpie carries the fire of the troubadours into Italy.

stops.name: Assisi, the merchant's house by San Nicolò
stops.campa: Assisi rises rose-colored on its spur of Subasio, and in the upper city, by San Nicolò off the Piazza del Comune, Pietro's house and warehouse receive his French bride. The town styles her Domina, the lady, from the first act to the last; her neighbors will remember her rank when they have forgotten his. Her dowry goes into the shop, and the shop begins to prosper as it never has. In the evenings she sings in the tongue Assisi half-knows from the fairs, and the merchant's house acquires the one thing it never had: a court.

stops.name: Assisi, the vision in pregnancy
stops.campa: Pica is with child, and Pietro rides for France, to the fairs of Beaucaire and Champagne, to trade until the season turns. In his absence the vision comes: her son will be a great spiritual leader, and his instrument will be the gaya ciencia of the troubadours, the art her whole life has carried. And a pilgrim's word attends it: the child must be born as the Lord was born, among the beasts, on straw. Pica does not receive the sentence as a humiliation. She receives it as a libretto, and begins to plan a performance.

stops.name: Assisi, the ground floor emptied into a manger
stops.campa: In the days before her time, Pica empties the ground floor of the house and dresses it as a manger: hay strewn, an ox and an ass led in, the beasts breathing in the dark like a canticle. It is the first presepe, staged by the mother forty-two years before her son dresses Greccio for Christmas Eve. The neighbors think necessity; she knows better: not a stable forced on a laboring woman, but Bethlehem installed on purpose, a poem without text. Assisi will keep the little stall as an oratory, with its verse cut in stone over the door.

stops.name: Assisi, the stall of San Francesco il Piccolino
stops.campa: In the stall she has prepared, while Pietro trades in France, Pica is delivered of a son amid hay and under the gaze of the animals, born into a performance of the birth of the Lord, the recreation his mother staged for him. She has dreamed he will be a leader; she names him Giovanni for the Baptist, the desert herald, as another Elizabeth named her son John. The child draws his first breath inside his mother's theatre. Everything he will do, the crib at Greccio, the Canticle, the theatre of rags, begins inside this room.

stops.name: Assisi, the pilgrim at the door
stops.campa: A pilgrim comes begging at the door of the house where the child lies newborn, and will not take his alms and go: he must see the boy. The lady orders him satisfied. He takes the infant in his arms like old Simeon in the Temple, embraces and blesses him, and presses the sign of the cross into the right shoulder; then he is not there. Two children, he has said, were born this day in this street: one shall be among the best men of the world, and the other among the worst. Pica keeps all these sayings in her heart.
stops.quote: Afferte puerum ut videat — bring the child, that he may see him.
stops.quote_source: Liber exemplorum Fratrum Minorum §116 (c. 1280-1310; FA:ED III, 800, the only early source that names her)

stops.name: Assisi, Cathedral of San Rufino, the baptism
stops.campa: Carried up the hill to the cathedral of the martyr-bishop, the son of Pica is baptized Giovanni at the great Romanesque font, the mother's chosen name laid on him in water and the Holy Ghost. A stranger stands godfather, some say the same pilgrim, some say an angel in pilgrim's dress, and where he kneels the stone keeps the print of his knees, still shown beside the font. The same basin will christen Clare di Favarone and, tradition adds, the boy who becomes Emperor Frederick II. Like Elizabeth before her, Pica has given the Baptist's name against all custom of the father's house.

stops.name: Assisi, Pietro's return and the renaming
stops.campa: Pietro rides home from France with good profits and hears that in his absence he has a son named for the Baptist. He overrules the font: the boy shall be called Francesco. The father means the country of his business; but the house knows what the name honors: the mother. Francesco, the Frenchman: for her French culture, the romantic poetry of the troubadours, the exquisite cloth of Provence, and the family Bourlémont. Bonaventure will square the two hereafter: the boy kept the name his father gave him, and never abandoned the meaning of the name his mother gave.
stops.quote: Quid de filio meo putatis? Adhuc erit filius Dei per gratiam. — What do you think my son will be? Know that he will yet be a son of God by grace.
stops.quote_source: Legend of the Three Companions 2 (Latin critical edition, 1899)

stops.name: Assisi, San Giorgio, letters and Latin
stops.campa: Pica gives her son to the canons of San Giorgio by the walls, where hospital and school stand together, for his letters: Latin, the psalter, the clear hand her own canons of Brixey once gave her. He is an indifferent clerk and a quick singer; the Latin takes, but slantwise, the way it takes in a jongleur. Over this school's ground his body will one day lie four years while the great basilica is building, and Clare's church will rise upon it. The mother walks him home past the piazza, translating the day's lesson into Provençal, and setting it to a tune.

stops.name: Assisi, the loaves for the poor
stops.campa: At the merchant's table the boy heaps up loaves as though for a garrison and gives them at the door to the poor. The household grumbles; it is tolerated, the legend says, because his mother loved him more than the other children. There are other children now: Angelo, who will one day mock his brother's rags in the piazza; yet Assisi's ledgers will style him all his life not Angelo di Pietro but Angelo di Pica, the magpie's son. In this house the mother's name outweighs the father's, and the bread of the poor is the first economy her son learns.

stops.name: Monte Subasio, the voice of nature
stops.campa: She takes him up the mountain above the city, into the holm-oaks and the high meadow, and teaches him the third grammar after Latin and Provençal: the voice of nature. Wind, water, larks; the animals that do not care for fine French cloth and come instead to a tender voice, a soft look, a listening touch. She tells him of Giles the hermit of her own Provence road, who drank the red hind's milk and took the arrow in his flesh to shield her. Brother Sun and Sister Water are on this mountain already, waiting to be named.
